A_target.statement:
Let $\sequence {f_n}$ be a [[Definition:Uniformly Bounded|uniformly bounded]], [[Definition:Equicontinuous|equicontinuous]] sequence in $\map C {\closedint a b}$.
Then $\sequence {f_n}$ has a [[Definition:Uniform Convergence|uniformly convergent]] [[Definition:Subsequence|subsequence]].

B_source.statement:
Let $D = \set {d_1, d_2, \ldots}$ be [[Definition:Countable Set|countable]] and $\sequence {f_n}$ a sequence of functions on $D$ with $\sequence {\map {f_n} {d_k} }_n$ bounded for each $k$.
Then, extracting nested subsequences for $d_1, d_2, \ldots$ in turn and taking the diagonal, some subsequence converges at every point of $D$.

derived.equicontinuity: the mechanism upgrading convergence on D to uniform convergence

object_map.reformulation: Get convergence on a countable dense set by the diagonal argument, then spread it uniformly using equicontinuity and compactness.

validity_conditions: Uniform boundedness gives bounded values at each point, as the diagonal argument requires.
Equicontinuity and compactness of [a, b] are needed to pass from the dense set to all points uniformly.
Completeness of C([a, b]) under the supremum norm gives the limit.
proof_plan:
Let $D = \Q \cap \closedint a b$, which is countable and [[Definition:Everywhere Dense|dense]].
By the source result, with the [[Bolzano-Weierstrass Theorem]] at each point, some subsequence $\sequence {g_k}$ converges at every $d \in D$.

Let $\epsilon > 0$.
By equicontinuity, choose $\delta > 0$ with $\size {x - y} < \delta \implies \size {\map {f_n} x - \map {f_n} y} < \dfrac \epsilon 3$ for all $n$.

By compactness, finitely many $d_1, \ldots, d_m \in D$ are within $\delta$ of every point of $\closedint a b$.
Choose $K$ such that $\size {\map {g_k} {d_j} - \map {g_l} {d_j} } < \dfrac \epsilon 3$ for all $k, l \ge K$ and $j \le m$.

For any $x$, choosing $d_j$ with $\size {x - d_j} < \delta$ gives $\size {\map {g_k} x - \map {g_l} x} < \epsilon$ for $k, l \ge K$.
So $\sequence {g_k}$ is uniformly Cauchy, and converges uniformly as $\map C {\closedint a b}$ is [[Definition:Complete Metric Space|complete]].
This is the [[Arzelà-Ascoli Theorem]].
{{qed}}
